title: Timeout

validation.research: Six primary references: Michael Nygard’s Release It! publisher catalog lists Timeouts under stability patterns; Marc Brooker’s AWS article supports timeout selection, scarce-resource retention, phase coverage and retry risks; the gRPC deadline guide distinguishes timeout duration from a deadline and describes propagation/clock handling/server cancellation; Gráinne Sheerin’s gRPC article establishes possible disagreement between server success and client expiry; official Python 3.11 task/timeout and event-loop documentation supports cooperative cancellation, timeout_at semantics, cleanup, and local monotonic timing. Timeout is canonical and Timeouts is the plural catalog alias. Deadline is a related representation rather than a duplicate alias article. Quote scenario, budget arithmetic, mock dependencies, code and diagrams are original teaching material.

runnable_example.verification: Actual article fences run unchanged on Python 3.11+. Exact four-line demo output; malformed, Boolean, negative, nonfinite and excessive budgets reject before work; zero expires before callable creation; positive integer, float and 60000 ms maximum accepted. Controlled-clock accounting with real timeout contexts proves one deadline for serial stages, 120 ms leaves 180 ms of a 300 ms budget, exact equality and overrun prevent the next stage, and an overdue second-stage return is rejected. Native asyncio timers expire during each phase; explicitly gated awaited cleanup proves the caller remains pending until cleanup finishes and observes TimeoutError afterward, with no detached work. Dependency ConnectionError and dependency-origin TimeoutError preserve identity without attributing them to this timer. External caller cancellation propagates as CancelledError after cleanup, with no false TimeoutError conversion. A cleanup exception overrides timeout and preserves cancellation context. Blocking synchronous work returns before explicit expiry checks reject its late result, demonstrating no preemption. A dependency that suppresses one cancellation still cannot publish an overdue value; no guarantee is inferred for indefinite suppression. Current-task cancellation state clears, independent calls succeed after errors, legitimate zero-valued business data remains distinct from timeout, all owned jobs are observed, and task inventory returns to baseline. Tests do not claim real-time return bounds, actual network cancellation, remote rollback, thread termination or retry safety.

example_limits: Original Python 3.11+ serial quote wrapper using one loop.time-based deadline and asyncio.timeout_at in the caller task. Zero-argument async stock and shipping callables share a numeric 0–60000 millisecond budget; Boolean, negative, oversized and nonfinite values reject before work. Zero or exact expiry prevents new work; explicit checks reject overdue synchronous returns and prevent starting shipping after inventory consumes the budget. Success returns an item count and a fee in cents. Cooperative stalled shipping yields to cancellation and runs a finally marker before TimeoutError handling. No detached child tasks or actual network connections are created. Cleanup and cancellation resistance can extend elapsed return time; this is not forced termination, remote rollback, safe retry, process isolation, a network client or a hard wall-clock guarantee. Verification combines controlled-clock accounting (while retaining real timeout contexts) with native timer expiry during both phases, awaited cleanup gates proving delayed caller completion, dependency-error identity, caller cancellation, cleanup exceptions and cancellation context, blocking synchronous returns, one-time cancellation suppression, cleared cancellation counters, independent calls and unchanged task inventory. The finally print models cleanup and the mocks open no sockets or remote connections. There is no latency benchmark, forced termination, remote rollback, thread killing or retry-safety guarantee.
